analysis.one_liner: Taxed oil companies' windfall profits and sent the money back to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2005 with 8 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged the large integrated oil companies an excise tax of 50% on profits above $40 a barrel, adjusted for inflation, for three years, while crediting new drilling, refinery, and renewable-fuel investment against the tax. Every dollar collected would have been rebated to individual taxpayers as an annual energy consumer rebate. Introduced in September 2005, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers: every filer would have received an annual rebate of up to the prior year's income and payroll tax liability, with the per-person amount set by how much the oil tax collected. The money came from the large integrated oil companies' profits above a fixed baseline, returning a share of their windfall to households during a stretch of high gasoline prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers hit by high gas prices

how_it_helps.text: Imposed an excise tax on integrated oil companies equal to 50% of the windfall profit on each barrel of crude — the amount the sales price exceeded $40 a barrel, adjusted for inflation — for three years.

Rebated the revenue to individual taxpayers as an annual energy consumer rebate of up to the taxpayer's prior-year income and payroll tax liability, with the amount determined by total collections and paid shortly after February 1 each year.

Allowed companies to offset the tax dollar-for-dollar with investment in drilling costs, refinery capacity, and renewable electricity or ethanol and biodiesel facilities, so windfall revenue could be redirected into expanding supply.
Excluded oil from newly discovered fields, made the windfall tax deductible, and applied only to integrated oil companies rather than independent producers.

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies — the large firms that produce, refine, and sell crude — would have paid 50% of profits above $40 a barrel for three years, unless they invested the money in drilling, refineries, or renewable fuels. Some of the tax could have been passed on to consumers through higher fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: A windfall tax on existing production can be passed on to consumers at the pump and can discourage drilling; the federal windfall profits tax of 1980 was later criticized for exactly that. This bill tried to blunt both problems — it exempted oil from newly discovered fields and let companies erase the tax through new drilling, refinery, and renewable-fuel investment — but those same carve-outs also shrank how much money would have been collected.

The rebate was capped at each household's prior-year income and payroll tax liability, so a household owing little or no federal tax would have received little or nothing; above the cap, every taxpayer got the same flat amount regardless of how much more they were paying for fuel.
Only integrated oil companies owed the tax, so production could shift toward exempt independent producers and newly discovered fields over the three-year window, shrinking collections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the arithmetic favored the bill: a temporary tax aimed at the largest oil firms' profits above a fixed baseline, with the proceeds returned as cash rebates while gasoline prices were squeezing family budgets. The design showed drafters had learned from the troubled 1980 windfall profits tax — new fields were exempt and new investment canceled the tax, reducing the risk of curbing domestic supply — but those carve-outs cut into the revenue. The honest weak points are pass-through (companies could raise prices to recover part of the tax) and the flat, liability-capped rebate, which protected households that already owed federal tax far more than those that did not.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, it never got a hearing or vote, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Byron Dorgan introduced the bill on September 7, 2005; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
The only recorded activity afterward was Dorgan speaking for the bill on the Senate floor on September 14 and 26, 2005 and February 15, 2006; the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote.
The bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without ever returning to the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies kept the windfall profits of 2005 and 2006 — among the most profitable years on record for the industry — with no new tax, and taxpayers received no rebate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Integrated oil companies, which kept the profits

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 7, 2005 and spoke for it repeatedly on the Senate floor in September 2005 and February 2006, the only actions ever recorded on the measure.

for.name: 8 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Chris Dodd and Barbara Boxer; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral on September 7, 2005 and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Publicly rejected the idea of a windfall profits tax on oil companies when rising gas prices made it a live issue in 2006.

sides.party_line_note: Every senator behind the bill — the sponsor and all 8 cosponsors — was a Democrat, the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it, and no roll-call vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 50% of their profits above $40 a barrel for three years, though they could cut the bill by investing in drilling, refineries, or renewable fuels. When it died in committee, the industry kept its 2005-06 windfall profits untaxed and consumers received nothing.

industries.industry: Renewable fuel and renewable electricity producers
industries.note: Oil companies could offset the windfall tax by building ethanol, biodiesel, and renewable electricity facilities, steering windfall money toward those industries and their suppliers.
